title: Hypertrophy Q&A #7
summary: Q&A covering bench variations (feet-up, EZ-bar monkey grip, Arnold press), burnout, when to add volume, atrophy, rep speed, deconditioning vs deloads, myo-reps, pullovers and rib cage, sandbagging vs quality tonnage, rear delts, belt squats, reverse-grip DB bench, skullcrusher elbows and hinge programming. Recurring themes: control every rep, add volume only when progress stalls, and avoid deloads/detraining.
claims: He never sets up in a disadvantaged position on bench; the feet-up (Larsen) press kills his arch so he doesn't use it
His number one priority when benching is keeping the shoulders safe and set; if he can't, he doesn't bench
Feet-up bench removes leg drive so you lift less and must brace hard through the core for stability, which can make it a useful variation, but it is not a must-do
Avoid the false (suicide) grip on heavy horizontal pressing because the bar can roll; on vertical presses the bar stacks over the forearm and false grip is excellent

EZ-bar close-grip press with a monkey grip is a good backup movement and pairs well after skullcrushers, but it is not strength-work material and doesn't beat a standard barbell close-grip bench; watch elbow comfort
The Arnold press is a gimmicky hybrid lift: fine at the end of an arm or press day but too random to bank progress on; he would not program it
If you want shoulder or wrist rotation work, do it separately with light weight as mobility rather than mixing it into a press

Baki physiques escalate each arc like pro bodybuilding: early Baki looked fairly natty with big legs and core, later came huge calves and leaner builds, and in Son of Ogre everything is huge, losing some charm
You don't 'feel' like you're not gaining weight: it's measurable; if the scale isn't moving, add a snack such as a bowl of rice with chicken (about 200 kcal)
Skinny guys who can't gain weight have only themselves to blame; there is always a cheap, easy way to eat more
Naturals are better protected from burnout and injury because drugs don't mask the body's signals; gym acquaintances on deca felt great, came off and discovered injuries they had worsened
Burnout usually means doing too much in the gym and too little outside it; lanky high-metabolism lifters need less work than they think, so cut volume and raise calories
Lifting can be strenuous without being stressful; make the gym a happy, meditative place; for him training relieves stress
If you spend the last 30-40 minutes of a 90-minute session drained and going through the motions, the workout is too long; shorten it and make it more intense
Too much volume can stop a muscle from growing: breaking it down again before it repairs is like re-sitting on a glued chair before the glue sets
Add volume only when progress stalls; if you are steadily progressing in weight you don't need to add any

Intensity rises automatically as load progresses, while volume and frequency are levers you pull only when needed; pushing intensity without tonnage growing means you are training for strength, not size
When stalled, add a variation, two back-off sets, or nucleus overload elsewhere in the week, staying within the line of specificity
During a month at his family's mountain home without a gym, his leg size barely changed but his strength dropped hard, around 60 lb off his lifts, along with work capacity
Detrained strength isn't lost muscle but wasted time; atrophy can be reversed by hypertrophy

Neither chasing the mind-muscle feel nor moving the weight as fast as possible is the goal; the crux is moving a challenging weight with proper technique and full control, every rep identical in speed
Don't drop fast and rebound on the negative ('overspeed eccentrics'); that invites injury; control the negative without exaggerating, then drive up within reason
If the bar bounces off your back on squats or flies away from you on deadlifts, the weight is too light
The powerlifting idea that warm-ups must be moved explosively is placebo; warm-ups are for warming up, not blasting 25% of your max
A 13-day 'strategic deconditioning' break is just planned detraining: you lose neural adaptation, come back weaker and waste time and tonnage
He is against deloads: they come from powerlifting, and if a bodybuilding program needs one it is badly programmed and a sign of overuse
Myo-reps, like other finishers, are a cherry on top, not high-quality tonnage; programming them as top sets is unacceptable
Rib cage expansion with pullovers works because the tissue between ribs can expand; his lat spread changed dramatically in one year
His one tip for a better-looking back physique: do pullovers
Waking with numb arms is harmless if sensation returns; a truly pinched nerve, however, can cause atrophy and sometimes need surgery
For nerve issues use elastic-band nerve decompression drills and change sleeping position or pillow so the arm isn't trapped

Sandbagging isn't inherently bad: it is bad when it replaces quality tonnage outside a relevant intensity window, and good when it is planned RIR or reduced volume because the muscle is trained again in two days
Back-off sets are judged against the fatigued in-workout baseline, not the fresh 1RM; taken to failure in a relevant rep range they are quality tonnage
If you front squat 200 lb x5 fresh and still get 200 x5 easily after back squats, the back-off set isn't near failure; raise the weight
If your back squat max is 400 lb and late in the workout 180 lb for 3 is nearly impossible, you've dug too deep and the work is no longer relevant
Three sets of a first compound plus three of a second for the same muscle is plenty; adding a third variation is extreme fatigue, not needed for hypertrophy
Face pulls and rows are not the best rear delt builders; presses and raises are better, and his favorite rear delt movement is what he calls Arnold raises
Band reverse laterals work the rear delt but are hard to load and tend to be junk volume
Flat pullovers tension lats and chest at the bottom due to leverage; decline pullovers add range but the stretch starts later; for decline use an EZ bar, or do both as main lift and variation

The belt squat gives free quad tonnage with near-zero injury risk since it tractions the lower back; the danger is the setup, and cable-loaded belt squats pull you out of position more than plate-loaded ones
Program belt squats for 4 sets of 10-15 or 8-12, never low reps; use them on hinge day after deadlifts (superset with pull-ups) or after back squats when the lower back is fried
Reverse-grip dumbbell bench is shoulder-friendly; press straight or slightly outward, never converging inward
Rotate reverse-grip and regular dumbbell bench rather than doing both: regular at higher intensity, reverse for volume; detraining between them is minimal

Elbow flare is just a visual cue: on presses it signals internal rotation or touching too high, but on skullcrushers flaring is fine; he flares a lot to feel the triceps stretch, while tucked elbows load his tendons
Keep heavy hinge work as far as possible from deadlift day in the week; he dislikes rotating deadlifts between intensity and volume because he prefers stability in strength work
Never do RDLs and good mornings on the same day: both are hinges loading the lower back, a recipe for injury; rotate them week to week instead
